title: Hash-Based Indexing
lead: Follow how a hash index assigns keys to buckets, then see how the buckets and directory change as data is added.
goals: Explain in-memory hashing and collision resolution
Trace searches, insertions, deletions, and overflow in static chained hashing
Recognise skew and identify when rehashing is needed
Simulate global and local depth, bucket splits, and directory changes in extendible hashing

sections.title: Ask the right questions of a hash index
sections.html:
A hash index applies a hash function to assign each key to a bucket, a storage area for entries with the same hash address. Two keys in the same bucket must still be compared directly. This approach suits equality lookups, which search for a key with a particular value. For a range query, keys that are close in value need not be close together after hashing.

Original worked example: divide each ticket code by 4 and use the remainder as its bucket number. In compact notation, h(k)=k mod 4, where k is the ticket code and h(k) is a bucket number from 0 to 3. Codes 6, 10, and 14 all enter bucket 2. Finding code 10 requires checking the entries in that bucket; finding every code from 6 to 14 cannot be done by reading bucket 2 alone. Chaining links entries into a list; open addressing searches for another slot in an in-memory table. In a database, a bucket commonly occupies one or more pages.

Key takeaway

The same hash does not mean the same key. Hashing narrows down where to look; key comparisons are still needed to confirm a match.

Related source material: PDF pages 2–6. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Static hashing: overflow determines the cost
sections.html:
Keep a fixed set of 4 primary bucket pages, each holding 2 entries. Inserting 6 and 10 fills bucket 2; inserting 14 requires an overflow page, an additional page linked to a full bucket. Looking up 14 may read 2 pages even though the hash function runs only once. Insertions and deletions must also write any modified pages. As the data grows, overflow chains lengthen; as it shrinks, some buckets may be left empty.

Rehashing recalculates the location of every entry using a new bucket mapping. Increasing the number of buckets redistributes the data but requires many page reads and writes. A fast hash function is not enough: a skewed key distribution or many duplicate keys can still create hot spots. The modulo function above is an illustration, not the best choice for every dataset.

Related source material: PDF pages 7–12. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Extendible hashing: grow where space is needed
sections.html:
Extendible hashing uses a directory, a table of pointers to buckets. The global depth g is the number of hash bits used to look up a directory entry; the local depth d is the number of bits that identify a particular bucket. The example below uses the trailing bits, or suffix.

Original worked example: g=2 gives 4 directory pointers labelled 00, 01, 10, and 11. Bucket 01 has d=2, holds at most 2 entries, and currently contains hash values 1 (001) and 5 (101). Inserting 9 (1001) exceeds its capacity, so split it using the last 3 bits. Bucket 001 receives 1 and 9; bucket 101 receives 5. Both new buckets have d=3, which exceeds the old g=2, so the directory grows from 4 to 8 pointers.

Key takeaway

Doubling the directory enlarges only the pointer table. This step splits the full bucket; it does not copy every data bucket.

If the bucket has d<g before splitting, the directory already has enough bits to distinguish the two new buckets, so only the relevant pointers change. For example, with g=3 and d=1, the remaining 2 bits have 4 combinations, so 4 pointers refer to that bucket. In general, the number of pointers is 2^(g−d). Deletion may allow buckets to merge and the directory to shrink when the structural conditions permit it.

Related source material: PDF pages 13–25. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

sections.title: Check your understanding with a trace
sections.html:
With global depth g=3 and a bucket whose local depth is d=1, how many pointers refer to that bucket? Does splitting it once require doubling the directory?

Show the solution

There are 2^(3−1)=4 pointers. After the split, each new bucket has d=2 and receives 2 pointers. No doubling is needed because 2≤3. If several keys have exactly the same complete hash value, adding bits cannot separate them; a practical implementation needs a separate way to handle this case.

Related source material: PDF pages 15–25. The numerical examples and exercises in this section are original supplementary material.

quiz.question: A bucket with local depth 2 and global depth 4 is split into buckets with local depth 3. Which statement is correct?
options: The directory does not need to double
quiz.explanation: The new local depth, 3, still does not exceed the global depth, 4.
